takeaways: The Twin Cities market isn't crashing: the metro median sale price reached a record of about $410,000, with Minneapolis itself in the mid to high $300,000s. Homes are taking longer to sell (about 42 days, almost 8% longer than a year earlier), and price cuts are common.

Many sellers who won't come down bought in 2020 to 2022, when prices rose fast. After paying the costs of selling, they may be close to breaking even, so a $20,000 price cut can mean bringing money to closing.
Jason estimates the cost of selling at 8% to 10% of the price, including agent fees, closing costs, repairs and getting the home ready: $30,000 to $40,000 on a home in the $400,000s.
Low mortgage rates keep owners in place. Research Jason cites finds each percentage point between an owner's rate and today's rate makes them about 18% less likely to sell.
Owners who bought after spring 2022 at 7% or higher aren't held by their rate but by the price they paid. They're motivated but stuck.
For buyers: ask what the seller needs in order to sell, not just what the home is worth. Their purchase date and likely loan balance shape which offers can work.
For anyone buying now: know your exit plan, build in room for selling costs, and don't let a deadline make the decision.

faq.q: Is the Minneapolis housing market crashing?
faq.a: Not according to the numbers in this video: the metro median sale price hit a record of about $410,000. Homes are taking longer to sell and price cuts are more common, so buyers have more room to negotiate than in 2020 to 2022.

faq.q: How much does it cost to sell a house in the Twin Cities?
faq.a: Jason estimates 8% to 10% of the sale price once agent fees, closing costs, repairs and preparation are added up, or $30,000 to $40,000 on a home in the $400,000s. Ask for a net sheet with your own numbers.

faq.q: Why won't some sellers lower their price?
faq.a: Many bought near the 2020 to 2022 peak. After selling costs, a lower price could mean bringing money to closing, so they hold out for a number that lets them walk away clean.

takeaways: Mystery Cove, the indoor water park at the Mall of America, is planned to open in 2029: about 143,000 square feet with a wave pool, a 1,400-foot lazy river, more than 30 slides and a retractable roof, connected to the mall by skyway.

The water park itself is about $375 million, and more than $400 million with parking and infrastructure. In September 2025 Bloomington approved $160 million in tax increment financing, after a 2025 state law allowed it, alongside private loans.

The mall draws about 32 million visitors a year, about 40% of them from more than 150 miles away. The water park is projected to add almost a million visits a year, many staying overnight in Bloomington's more than 9,000 hotel rooms.

The homes nearest the effect are in Bloomington, Richfield, Eagan and South Minneapolis. Jason cites Bloomington's median at about $379,000 (Redfin, December 2025) and Richfield in the low to mid $300,000s.
Much of Bloomington's housing was built from the 1950s to the 1970s, so expect renovation and rebuilding on good lots as land values rise.
Signals to watch before 2029: construction milestones from 2026 to 2028, new hotels near the mall and I-494, and new housing proposals in Bloomington's South Loop district.

faq.q: When does the Mall of America water park open?
faq.a: Mystery Cove is planned to open in 2029, with construction starting in spring 2026, according to the video.

faq.q: How big is the Mall of America water park?
faq.a: About 143,000 square feet, with a wave pool, a 1,400-foot lazy river, more than 30 slides and attractions and a retractable roof, designed for about 3,000 guests at a time.

faq.q: How is the Mall of America water park being paid for?
faq.a: With $160 million in tax increment financing that Bloomington approved in September 2025, plus private loans and loan guarantees from the mall's owner, Triple Five, according to the video.

takeaways: The Minneapolis market split in two in 2026. Prices were up about 6% from a year earlier, with homes selling in about 30 days, yet closed sales in the city fell 15.7% in early 2026.

Well-priced suburban homes kept moving fast: Eden Prairie homes drew around six offers and sold in under 30 days, and Chanhassen homes sold in about 17 days. Woodbury, Maple Grove and Lakeville were also competitive.

Downtown Minneapolis was the soft spot. In Loring Park, North Loop, Mill District, Elliot Park, Downtown West and Marcy-Holmes, homes took about four months to sell in early 2026, closed sales fell almost 18%, and sellers took about 5.7% below asking on average.
Condo association fees, from under $300 to $1,000 a month or more, can make a downtown condo cost as much each month as a suburban house.

Suburban buyers: be fully underwritten, not just pre-qualified, and ready to move. Downtown buyers: negotiate for rate buydowns, closing costs and price, and review the association's reserves, insurance and special assessments first.
Sellers everywhere: price right from day one. The first 14 days on the market get the most attention, and 2022 prices are no guide anymore.

faq.q: Is it a buyer's or seller's market in Minneapolis?
faq.a: Both, depending on where. Well-priced suburban homes in places like Eden Prairie and Chanhassen were still selling quickly with multiple offers, while downtown Minneapolis condos took months and sold below asking in early 2026.

faq.q: What should I check before buying a condo?
faq.a: The association's financials: reserves, insurance costs, past and planned special assessments, and the monthly fee. Low reserves in an older building are a warning sign for big assessments later.

takeaways: Minneapolis isn't crashing; it's sorting. In July, the city's median sale price was $375,000 (up 5.9%), closed sales rose 16.7% and pending sales 9.8%, but homes took about 41 days to sell, and about 53 in August, against about 28 a year earlier.

Buyers have more choice. The metro had more than 11,500 homes for sale in July (up 6.7%), Minnesota had more than 20,000, the most in seven years, and Minneapolis had about 3.1 months of supply. A home has to win on price and condition.
Activity is strongest at the top: Minnesota sales over $1 million rose 18%, while pending sales under $400,000 rose 3.7%. Four-bedroom homes outpaced two-bedroom homes.

Property tax levies are rising. As of the video, Minneapolis had proposed an 11.3% levy increase for 2027 (final budget in December), and Ramsey County, Saint Paul and Dakota County had proposed increases too.
Minnesota home insurance rose about 34% in 2025, to an average of about $3,530 a year. Many policies now use percentage wind and hail deductibles: 2% on a home insured for $400,000 is $8,000.

Under Minn. Stat. 513.55, sellers must disclose known material facts, including anything a buyer's inspection reveals if that deal falls apart. Testing for radon before listing avoids a surprise mid-deal.
Condo sales depend on the building: buyers get the resale disclosure certificate (Minn. Stat. 515B.4-107) and association financials, and can cancel within a short window after receiving them.

Several cities, including Minneapolis, Saint Paul, Richfield, Bloomington and St. Louis Park, require a Truth-in-Sale-of-Housing evaluation before listing, and the report is public. Fix common items like backflow preventers, smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, broken windows and peeling paint first.

faq.a: A pre-listing evaluation some Minnesota cities require, including Minneapolis, Saint Paul, Richfield, Bloomington and St. Louis Park. The seller hires a city-licensed evaluator, the report becomes public, and required repairs must be made or taken on by the buyer. It doesn't replace a buyer's own inspection.

faq.q: Do I have to test for radon when selling a home in Minnesota?
faq.a: Minnesota doesn't require a test, but sellers must disclose radon test results and mitigation systems they know about. Testing before you list lets you deal with a high reading on your own schedule instead of mid-deal.

faq.q: Why are homes taking longer to sell in Minneapolis?
faq.a: More homes are for sale, so buyers can be pickier, and higher rates, insurance and property taxes stretch budgets. Homes that win on both price and condition still sell quickly.

takeaways: Treat a home as a long-term investment: some homes that look like deals are hard to finance, insure or sell later.

Older homes (common in Minneapolis, Saint Paul, Richfield and St. Louis Park): budget for what you can't see, such as wiring, plumbing, drain tile and the sewer line. Orangeburg fiber sewer pipe, used from about the 1940s to the 1970s, can collapse.
A sewer camera inspection costs about $200, while a sewer line repair from house to street can run $15,000 to $20,000, according to Jason. Get one on almost any home.

New construction: compare the builder's lender offer with another lender side by side. Know whether a rate buydown is permanent or temporary (a 2-1 buydown rises in year three). Get upgrades and incentives in writing, ask about future phases and association dues, and still hire an inspector.
In one Lakeville example, a new $365,000 townhome with a 5% builder rate had a lower payment than a 20-year-old $300,000 townhome at almost 7%.

Minnesota's new-home warranty runs 1 year on most of the home, 2 years on plumbing, electrical and heating systems, and 10 years on major structural defects. Schedule a walkthrough before the first year ends.
Condos: you share the building's costs. Check reserves and special assessments, and know that lenders must approve the building, which can limit future buyers.
Homes with no basement (slab-on-grade) and very unusual or ultra-modern designs can work well, but they narrow the pool of future buyers and can complicate appraisals.

faq.q: Should I get a sewer scope inspection?
faq.a: Yes, especially on older homes. It costs about $200 and can find a damaged or collapsing sewer line, a repair Jason puts at $15,000 to $20,000, before you buy.

faq.q: What does the Minnesota new home warranty cover?
faq.a: One year for defects in workmanship and materials, two years for plumbing, electrical and heating systems, and ten years for major structural defects, starting at closing.

faq.q: Is a builder's low mortgage rate a good deal?
faq.a: It can be, but compare it with an outside lender's offer side by side, check whether the buydown is permanent or temporary, and look at the price and closing costs, not just the payment.

takeaways: Jason has lived in Minneapolis for 49 years. The best part is the outdoors: the Chain of Lakes, the 50-mile Grand Rounds trail loop, Theodore Wirth Park's 759 acres, and more than 180 city parks.
St. Anthony Falls is the only natural major waterfall on the Mississippi, and 53-foot Minnehaha Falls is a neighborhood park.

The Twin Cities have a deep base of headquarters: Target, 3M, General Mills, UnitedHealth Group, U.S. Bank and Best Buy, plus Cargill, the largest privately held company. MSP is Delta's second-largest hub, with nonstop flights to Europe and Asia.
Home prices as of early 2026, as stated in the video: a median of about $350,000 in Minneapolis and about $290,000 in Saint Paul.

The trade-offs: high taxes (a top state income tax rate of 9.85% and property taxes Jason puts around 1.3% in Minneapolis), long winters with 50-plus inches of snow and short December days, heavy road salt and constant road construction.
Downtown office values have fallen sharply; Jason cites a building that sold for $200 million less than a decade ago and recently sold for about $6.25 million.
What's coming: the Green Line Extension to Eden Prairie (2027), the Blue Line Extension to Brooklyn Park, Highland Bridge in Saint Paul, and office-to-housing conversions downtown.

faq.q: What is the biggest downside of living in Minneapolis?
faq.a: For most people, the winters: 50-plus inches of snow, cold snaps and short December days. Jason also points to high income and property taxes and frequent road construction.

faq.q: How many lakes are in Minneapolis?
faq.a: Jason counts 22 lakes within city limits, including the Chain of Lakes, with Lake Minnetonka (about 14,000 acres) roughly 15 minutes west.
